chapter.title: Choosing Keys
chapter.description: What keys are for and why the array index is usually the wrong choice.

blocks.text: A `key` tells React which element in the new list corresponds to which element in the old list. Without it, React can only match by position, and position changes whenever items move.
What a good key looks like

items: **Stable** - the same item keeps the same key across renders.
**Unique** among siblings - it does not need to be globally unique.
**Predictable** - derived from the data, not generated during render.

blocks.text: Why the index breaks
Using the index means the key describes a position, not an item. Insert something at the top and every key shifts by one, so React thinks every item changed.
With plain text that is only wasteful. With components holding state - a checked box, a half-typed input, an open menu - that state ends up attached to the wrong row.
The index is safe only when the list never reorders, never has items inserted or removed, and the items hold no state. If you are not certain of all three, use a real id.
When there is no id
Generate ids when you create the items, not while rendering. A key created during render is new every time, which defeats the purpose entirely.
Keys are a hint to React, not a prop. A component cannot read its own `key`. If the child needs the value, pass it again under a different name.

blocks.text: React renders arrays by rendering each item in order, so the usual way to display a collection is `map`.

Use an arrow function with an implicit return - `(product) => (...)` - and no `return` keyword is needed. If you write `{` after the arrow you must return explicitly, which is a very common silent bug.
Filtering and sorting
Chain array methods before mapping. Copy before sorting, because `sort` mutates the array it is called on.
Empty states
An empty array renders nothing at all, which usually looks like a broken page. Handle it explicitly.

blocks.text: A **controlled** input takes its value from state and reports changes back through `onChange`. React holds the truth and the DOM just displays it.
Because the value lives in state, you can validate it, transform it, or reset it from anywhere.
Passing `value` without `onChange` gives you a read-only field and a console warning. Add the handler, or use `defaultValue` if you genuinely want an uncontrolled input.
The different field types
One state object for a whole form
Rather than a `useState` per field, many forms keep one object and a shared change handler. The `name` attribute picks the field to update.
Never initialise a controlled input to `undefined` or `null`. React starts it as uncontrolled and warns loudly when a value appears later. Use an empty string.
